Bonnets
BON-its
noun
From Old French bonet, a cap; rendering Hebrew pe’ērīm, an ornamental headdress — worn by Aaron’s sons “for glory and for beauty,” and by Zion’s daughters for vanity.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The bonnet leads the third line of Isaiah’s inventory: “The bonnets, and the ornaments of the legs, and the headbands, and the tablets, and the earrings” (Isa 3:20). But this headdress has a double life in Scripture, and the doubleness is the doctrine. The very same adornment was commanded for the priests: “for Aaron’s sons thou shalt make coats… and bonnets shalt thou make for them, for glory and for beauty” (Exo 28:40); and the bridegroom of Isaiah 61 “decketh himself with ornaments” — the same Hebrew word, a pe’ēr (Isa 61:10). One word, two heads: on the servant of the sanctuary it is glory; on the haughty street it is plunder for the seizure-list. Ornament, then, is not the sin; unconsecrated ornament is. Glory God assigns to an office He delights in; glory the self assigns to the self He inventories. The gospel does not end the bonnet but restores it: to them that mourn in Zion the LORD promises “beauty for ashes” — literally a pe’ēr for ashes (Isa 61:3), the festal headdress set on repentant heads by God’s own hand. Let the believer wear nothing he has crowned himself with; the only glory that survives the inventory is the glory God Himself sets on.

Webster 1828 Definition

One headdress, two heads: commanded on priests “for glory and for beauty,” inventoried on the haughty — glory is safe only where God assigns it.

Commanded for Aaron’s sons “for glory and for beauty” (Exo 28:40).

Key Scripture

Isa 3:20 — "The bonnets, and the ornaments of the legs, and the headbands, and the tablets, and the earrings,"

Exo 28:40 — "And for Aaron's sons thou shalt make coats, and thou shalt make for them girdles, and bonnets shalt thou make for them, for glory and for beauty."

Isa 61:3 — "To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified."

Isa 61:10 — "I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels."

Modern Corruption

The bonnet splits the age’s confusion about glory: adornment God assigns is holy; adornment the self assigns to the self goes on the seizure-list.

expand to see more

The corruption is self-coronation. The same headdress that was holy on a priest was plunder on the proud, and the difference was never the fabric but the assigning hand. The present age knows only self-assigned glory — self-styled, self-titled, self-crowned — and cannot imagine beauty as something conferred rather than claimed.

The recovered principle is glory by assignment. God delights to beautify: He commanded bonnets for glory and for beauty, and He promises the festal pe’er for ashes to them that mourn. The believer refuses every crown of his own weaving and receives what God sets on — for the only ornament that survives the inventory is the one His hand bestowed.

Hebrew Roots

Rendering the Hebrew pe’erim, bonnets crown both the consecrated priest and the haughty daughter — the assigning hand, not the fabric, decides which.
